title: Amritsar-Born Diplomat Tells Pakistan at UN: India Will Not Bow to Nuclear Blackmail
excerpt: Anmol Sher Singh Bedi, Senior Adviser (Disarmament) at India's Geneva mission, exercised India's right of reply at the UNGA First Committee, rejecting Pakistan's Kashmir claims and setting three red lines on terror and nuclear rhetoric.
body:
• Anmol Sher Singh Bedi, Senior Adviser (Disarmament) at India's Permanent Mission in Geneva and a native of Amritsar, exercised India's right of reply at the UN General Assembly's First Committee after Pakistan raised Jammu and Kashmir during a disarmament session.
  • Bedi said Jammu and Kashmir is "an integral and inalienable part of India," demanded Pakistan vacate what he called illegally occupied territory, and declared India "will not bow" to nuclear blackmail.
  • He laid out three red lines: any terror attack will meet a fitting response, no distinction will be made between terror sponsors and masterminds, and nuclear rhetoric will not shield cross-border terrorism.

An Amritsar-born Indian diplomat delivered a sharp rebuttal to Pakistan at the United Nations this week, warning that nuclear weapons cannot be used as a tool of everyday statecraft and declaring that India "will not bow" to nuclear blackmail.

Anmol Sher Singh Bedi, Senior Adviser (Disarmament) at India's Permanent Mission to the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva, exercised India's right of reply at a plenary meeting of the First Committee of the 81st UN General Assembly — the committee that handles disarmament and international security — after Pakistan's remarks raised the issue of Jammu and Kashmir. In a statement on X, Bedi wrote that "escalation concerns are best judged by conduct, not rhetoric."

What Bedi said

Bedi rejected Pakistan's claims outright, calling Jammu and Kashmir "an integral and inalienable part of India" and demanding that India's illegally occupied territories be vacated and returned. He stressed that India does not seek conflict but would hold attackers accountable. "India has always stood for peace and continues to seek peace with one and with all," he said. "However, if there is no accountability for reckless actions, then peace rarely becomes a pause between crises."

His sharpest lines were aimed at Pakistan's nuclear rhetoric. "Nuclear weapons must not be treated as routine instruments of statecraft," Bedi said. "A posture that relies on nuclear overhang to limit the consequences of subconventional activity raises the risk of escalation and not the prospect of restraint." He underlined that India's capabilities are defensive in nature, shaped by the country's own security environment, and directed against no state.

"We heard concerns about escalation. These are legitimate concerns. However, these are best judged by conduct over time. Nuclear weapons must not be treated as routine instruments of statecraft."

— Anmol Sher Singh Bedi, Indian diplomat

Three red lines

Bedi's response carried a trio of non-negotiable positions. First, measured self-defence: he described India's recent military actions as a targeted, non-escalatory response in self-defence following the Pahalgam terror attack that killed 26 civilians. Second, no distinction between terror sponsors and masterminds — support networks and perpetrators would be treated alike. Third, rejecting nuclear overhang: nuclear rhetoric cannot shield cross-border terrorism.

He also took aim at Pakistan's requests for nuclear cooperation, pointing to the A.Q. Khan proliferation network — the network accused of supplying nuclear bomb-making technology to other countries — and cited UN Security Council Resolution 1540, urging strict vigilance over advanced weapons transfers. On the Indus Waters Treaty, he signalled that the treaty relies on good faith and that a state cannot destroy trust while expecting treaty privileges to remain untouched.

The mechanism: how the right of reply works

The right of reply is a standard procedural tool at the UN: when one delegation makes remarks another considers objectionable, the aggrieved delegation can take the floor afterward to rebut on the record. India's permanent missions have made it a signature practice — young diplomats exercising the right of reply has become a familiar feature of UN sessions whenever Pakistan raises Kashmir, with Bedi following in a line that includes earlier rebuttals in the Sixth Committee (legal) and Third Committee (human rights) debates. Bedi's move this time was notable because it came in the First Committee, the disarmament body, where the nuclear dimension was unavoidable.

Pakistan's side

Bedi's rebuttal followed remarks by Pakistan's permanent representative in Geneva, Tahir Andarabi, who had raised the Jammu and Kashmir issue during the disarmament discussion. Pakistan's position — reiterated at multiple UN forums — is that Kashmir remains an unresolved dispute and that India's actions there violate international norms. India has consistently rejected that framing, holding that the entire region is an integral part of the country and that cross-border terrorism sponsored from Pakistani soil is the core obstacle to dialogue.

Why it matters for the diaspora

UNGA season is peak attention time for the global Indian diaspora, and Bedi's performance has already gone viral on social media — a reminder of how strongly India's diplomatic messaging resonates with Indians abroad. For diaspora readers, the red-line framework matters practically: the posture against nuclear blackmail shapes India's crisis response doctrine, and the insistence on accountability over mere restraint suggests any future terror incident would trigger a calibrated retaliatory response rather than a purely diplomatic one. Watch the First Committee's remaining sessions and India's October statements for follow-through on the vigilance agenda Bedi set.

items.text: No distinction between terror sponsors and masterminds.
Nuclear rhetoric cannot shield cross-border terrorism.
Jammu and Kashmir is integral to India.
Nuclear weapons must not be routine statecraft.
India seeks peace but demands accountability.
